title: Verbascum thapsus
wikitext:
{{Short description|Species of plant}} {{pp-move}} {{Use dmy dates|date=April 2026}} {{Speciesbox | image = Starr_040723-0030_Verbascum_thapsus.jpg | image_caption = Second-year plant starting to flower, with a dead stem of the previous year, behind left | genus = Verbascum | species = thapsus | authority = [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] }} '''''Verbascum thapsus''''', the '''great mullein''', '''greater mullein''' or '''common mullein''', is a species of [[Verbascum|mullein]] native to Europe, northern Africa, and Asia, and introduced in the Americas, Australia and New Zealand.{{cite web |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' (common mullein) |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/56652 |publisher=CABI |access-date=13 July 2019 |date=20 November 2018 |archive-date=8 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221008083319/https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/56652 |url-status=live }} It is a hairy [[biennial plant]] that can grow to 2 m tall or more. Its small, yellow flowers are densely grouped on a tall stem, which grows from a large [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]] of leaves. It grows in a wide variety of habitats, but prefers well-lit, disturbed soils, where it can appear soon after the ground receives light, from long-lived seeds that persist in the [[soil seed bank]]. It is a common [[weed]]y plant that spreads by prolifically producing seeds, and has become [[invasive species|invasive]] in temperate world regions. It is a minor problem for most agricultural crops, since it is not a competitive species, being intolerant of shade from other plants and unable to survive [[Tillage|tilling]]. It also hosts many insects, some of which can be harmful to other plants. Although individuals are easy to remove by hand, populations are difficult to eliminate permanently. Although commonly used in [[traditional medicine]], no [[approved drug]]s are made from this plant.{{cite web |title=Mullein |url=https://www.drugs.com/npp/mullein.html |publisher=Drugs.com |access-date=7 February 2021 |date=23 November 2020 }} It has been used to make [[dye]]s and [[torch]]es. == Description == [[Image:Starr 040723-0260 Verbascum thapsus.jpg|left|thumb|alt=|A stemless rosette in [[Hawaii]]]] ''V. thapsus'' is a [[dicotyledon]]ous plant that produces a [[rosette (botany)|rosette]] of leaves in its first year of growth.{{cite encyclopedia |last=Ferguson |first=Ian Keith |editor=Tutin, Thomas Gaskell |encyclopedia=[[Flora Europaea]] |title=''V. thapsus'' |year=1972 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |volume=3: Diapensiaceae to Myoporaceae |location=Cambridge |page=211 |isbn=0-521-08489-X |display-editors=etal }}Blamey, M., & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. Hodder & Stoughton, {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}. The leaves are large, up to 50 cm long. The second-year plants normally produce a single unbranched stem, usually 1–2 m tall. In the eastern part of its range in China, it is, however, only reported to grow up to 1.5 m tall.{{Cite web |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200021301 |work=Flora of China |publisher=eFloras.org |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-date=14 July 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090714055208/http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200021301 |url-status=live }} The tall, pole-like stems end in a dense [[raceme|spike]] of flowers that can occupy up to half the stem length. All parts of the plants are covered with star-shaped [[trichome]]s.{{cite web |last=Wetherwax |first=M. |year=1993 |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' L. |url=http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?7177,7595,7598 |work=Jepson Manual online |publisher=[[University of California at Berkeley]] |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-date=22 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171022142059/http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?7177,7595,7598 |url-status=live }} This cover is particularly thick on the leaves, giving them a silvery appearance. The species' [[chromosome number]] is 2n = 36. On flowering plants, the leaves are alternately arranged up the stem. They are thick and [[decurrent]], with much variation in leaf shape between the upper and lower leaves on the stem, ranging from [[leaf shape|oblong to oblanceolate]], and reaching sizes up to 50 cm long and 14 cm across (19 inches long and 5 inches wide).Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan. {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5 }} They become smaller higher up the stem, and less strongly decurrent down the stem. The flowering stem is solid and 2–2.5 cm (nearly an inch) across, and occasionally branched just below the [[inflorescence]], usually following damage.{{cite web |first=Marc C. |last=Hoshovsky |title=Element Stewardship Abstract for ''Verbascum thapsus'' |url=http://www.invasive.org/weedcd/pdfs/tncweeds/verbtha.pdf |date=August 2001 |publisher=The Global Invasive Species Initiative |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-date=13 May 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110513204304/http://www.invasive.org/weedcd/pdfs/tncweeds/verbtha.pdf |url-status=live }} After flowering and seed release, the stem and fruits usually persist in winter, drying into dark brown, stiff structures of densely packed, ovoid-shaped, and dry seed capsules. The dried stems may persist into the following spring or even the next summer. The plant produces a shallow [[taproot]]. [[Image:Starr 040723-0267 Verbascum thapsus.jpg|upright|thumb|alt=|A closeup of the flowers]] Flowers are pentamerous with (usually) five [[stamen]], a five-lobed [[calyx tube]], and a five-petalled [[Corolla (flower)|corolla]], the latter bright yellow and {{convert|1.5|–|3|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide. The flowers are almost [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]], with very short [[pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] (2 mm, 0.08 in). The five stamens are of two types, with the three upper stamens being shorter, their filaments covered by yellow or whitish hairs, and having smaller [[anther]]s, while the lower two stamens have [[Glossary of botanical terms#glabrous|glabrous]] filaments and larger anthers.They are all hairy in subspecies ''V. crassifolium'' and ''V. giganteum''. The plant produces small, ovoid (6 mm, 0.24 in) [[capsule (fruit)|capsules]] that split open by way of two valves, each capsule containing large numbers of minute, brown [[seed]]s less than 1 mm (0.04 in) in size, marked with longitudinal ridges. A white-flowered form, ''V. thapsus'' f. ''candicans'', is known to occur. Flowering lasts up to three months from early to late summer (June to August in northern Europe), with flowering starting at the bottom of the spike and progressing irregularly upward; each flower opens for part of a day and only a few open at the same time around the stem. == Taxonomy == For the purpose of [[botanical nomenclature]], ''Verbascum thapsus'' was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his 1753 ''{{lang|la|[[Species Plantarum]]}}''. The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''thapsus'' had been first used by [[Theophrastus]] (as {{lang|el|[[:wikt:Θάψος|Θάψος]]}}, ''{{lang|el|Thapsos}}'') for an unspecified herb from the [[Ancient Greece|Ancient Greek]] settlement of [[Thapsos]], near modern [[Syracuse, Sicily|Syracuse]], [[Sicily]],{{cite book |last=Carnoy |first=A. |title=Dictionnaire étymologique des noms grecs de plantes |year=1959 |location=Louvain |publisher=Publications Universitaires |oclc=3284108 |language=fr }}{{in lang|sv}} [http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/scrophularia/verba/verbtha.html Den virtuella Floran: ''Verbascum thapsus''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131112131031/http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/scrophularia/verba/verbtha.html |date=12 November 2013 }}, retrieved on 6 November 2009. though it is often assimilated to the ancient Tunisian city of [[Thapsus]].{{Cite web |last=Charters |first=Michael L. |title=Plant name: T |work=California Plant Names: Latin and Greek Meanings and Derivations |url=http://www.calflora.net/botanicalnames/pageT.html#thapsus |publisher=Calflora.net |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-date=28 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210228024000/http://www.calflora.net/botanicalnames/pageT.html#thapsus |url-status=live }} At the time, no [[type specimen]] was specified, as the practice only arose later, in the 19th century. When a lectotype (type selected amongst original material) was designated, it was assigned to specimen 242.1 of Linnaeus' herbarium, the only ''V. thapsus'' specimen.{{refn|The lectotypification is usually attributed to Arthur Huber-Morath (1971) ''Denkschriften der Schweizerischen Naturforschenden Gesellschaft'' 87:43. Some disagree since Huber-Morath did not specifically cite sheet 242.1, and credit instead L. H. Cramer, in Dassanayake & Fosberg (1981) ''A Revised Handbook to the Flora of Ceylon'' 3:389.{{Cite web |title=''Verbascum thapsus'': citation |url=http://www.florida.plantatlas.usf.edu/Plant.aspx?id=1757 |work=Atlas of Florida vascular Plants |publisher=Institute for Systematic Botany |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-date=14 June 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110614235400/http://www.florida.plantatlas.usf.edu/Plant.aspx?id=1757 |url-status=live }}|group=note}} The species had previously been designated as [[type species]] for ''[[Verbascum]]''.{{cite journal |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' |url=http://www.nhm.ac.uk/jdsml/research-curation/projects/linnaean-typification/detail.dsml?ID=925400 |journal=Linnaean Plant Name Typification Project |year=2022 |publisher=Natural History Museum |doi=10.5519/qwv6u7j5 |access-date=6 November 2009 |author1=Natural History Museum |archive-date=27 June 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080627171201/http://www.nhm.ac.uk/jdsml/research-curation/projects/linnaean-typification/detail.dsml?ID=925400 |url-status=live }} European plants exhibit considerable [[phenotype|phenotypical]] variation, which has led to the plant acquiring many [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]] over the years.{{Cite web |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' synonymy |url=http://www.northernontarioflora.ca/chklst.cfm?speciesid=1004482 |publisher=Northern Ontario Plant Database |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-date=19 March 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080319022523/http://www.northernontarioflora.ca/chklst.cfm?speciesid=1004482 |url-status=live }} Introduced American populations show much less variation. The taxonomy of ''Verbascum'' has not undergone any significant revision since Svanve Mürbeck's monographs in the 1930s, with the exception of the work of Arthur Huber-Morath, who used informal grouping in organizing the genus for the florae of Iran and Turkey to account for many intermediate species. Since Huber-Morath's groups are not taxonomical, Mürbeck's treatment is the most current one available, as no study has yet sought to apply genetic or molecular data extensively to the genus. In Mürbeck's classification, ''V. thapsus'' is placed in sect. ''Bothrospermae'' subsect. ''Fasciculata'' alongside species such as ''[[Verbascum nigrum]]'' (black or dark mullein), ''[[Verbascum lychnitis]]'' (white mullein), and ''[[Verbascum sinuatum]]'' (wavy-leaved mullein).{{cite journal |last1=Sotoodeh |first1=Arash |title=Verbascum oreophilum var. oreophilum and Verbascum cheiranthifolium var. asperulum (Scrophulariaceae) two new records for the flora of Iran |journal=Phytotaxa |date=2014 |volume=178 |issue=3 |pages=205–210 |doi=10.11646/phytotaxa.178.3.6 |bibcode=2014Phytx.178..205S |s2cid=86267331 }}{{cite journal |last1=Sotoodeh |first1=Arash |last2=Civeyrel |first2=L. |last3=Attar |first3=F. |title=''Verbascum shahsavarensis ''(Scrophulariaceae), a new species for Flora of Iran |journal=Phytotaxa |date=19 March 2015 |volume=203 |issue=1 |pages=76 |doi=10.11646/phytotaxa.203.1.8 |bibcode=2015Phytx.203...76S |url=http://publication.plazi.org/id/FFF1FFF2272AFFD1FFECFFD0FF9CFFCA }}{{cite journal |first1=Farideh |last1=Attar |first2=Atefeh |last2=Keshvari |first3=Ahmad |last3=Ghahreman |first4=Shahin |last4=Zarre |first5=Fatemeh |last5=Aghabeigi |display-authors=1 |year=2007 |title=Micromorphological studies on Verbascum (Scrophulariaceae) in Iran with emphasis on seed surface, capsule ornamentation and trichomes |journal=Flora – Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants |volume=202 |issue=2 |pages=169–175 |doi=10.1016/j.flora.2006.04.001 |bibcode=2007FMDFE.202..169A }} As ''Verbascum thapsus'' is the type species of the genus the application of article 22 of the [[ICNafp]] gives sect. ''Verbascum'' subsect. ''Verbascum'' as the correct nomenclature for this placement. === Subspecies and hybrids === {| class="wikitable floatright" style="clear:right; text-align:center; font-size:90%" |+ Hybrids of ''Verbascum thapsus''{{cite web |last=Stace |first=C. |author-link=Clive Stace |editor1-first=R. |editor1-last=van der Meijden |editor2-first=I. |editor2-last=de Kort |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' (Mullein, Great) |url=http://wbd.etibioinformatics.nl/bis/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=3577 |work=Interactive Flora of NW Europe |publisher=World Biodiversity Database |access-date=20 November 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120606145454/http://wbd.etibioinformatics.nl/bis/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=3577 |archive-date=6 June 2012 }}{{cite book |last=Kartesz |first=John |title=A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland (Volume 1: Checklist) |year=1994 |location=Portland, Oregon |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=0-88192-204-8 |page=588 }} |- !Hybrid name !Other

Murb.; Mediterranean region and to 2000 metres in southwestern Austria. (syn. subsp. ''montanum'' (Scrad.) Bonnier & Layens) * ''V. t. giganteum'' (Willk.) Nyman; Spain, endemic. In all subspecies but the type, the lower stamens are also hairy.{{cite web |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' L. subsp. ''montanum'' (Schrad.) Bonnier et layens |url=http://herbarivirtual.uib.es/cas-med/especie/4440.html |publisher=Universitat de les Illes Balears |work=Herbario Virtual del Mediterráneo Occidental |access-date=6 November 2009 |language=ca |archive-date=23 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090923192931/http://herbarivirtual.uib.es/cas-med/especie/4440.html |url-status=live }} In ''V. t. crassifolium'', the hairiness is less dense and often absent from the upper part of the anthers, while lower leaves are hardly decurrent and have longer petioles.{{cite book |last=Schmeil |first=Otto |author2=Fitschen, Jost |author3=Seybold, Siegmund |title=Flora von Deutschland, 93. Auflage |publisher=Quelle & Meyer Verlag |year=2006 |location=Wiebelsheim |isbn=3-494-01413-2 |page=496 }} In ''V. t. giganteum'', the hairs are densely white tomentose, and lower leaves are strongly decurrent. ''V. t. crassifolium'' also differs from the type in having slightly larger flowers, which measure 15–30 mm wide, whereas in the type, they are 12–20 mm in diameter. Both ''V. t. giganteum'' and ''V. t. crassifolium'' were originally described as species. Due to its morphological variation, ''V. thapsus'' has had a great many subspecies described. A recent revision led its author to maintain ''V. giganteum'' but sink ''V. crassifolium'' into synonymy.{{cite encyclopedia |last=Benedí Gonzalez |first=Carles |year=2009 |title=Verbascum |url=http://www.floraiberica.org/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/13_144_01_Verbascum.pdf |encyclopedia=[[Flora Iberica]] |volume=XIII: Plantaginaceae-Scrophulariaceae |pages=49–97 |location=Madrid |publisher=Real Jardín Botánico |isbn=978-84-00-08747-0 |language=es |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110513210128/http://www.floraiberica.org/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/13_144_01_Verbascum.pdf |archive-date=13 May 2011 }} The plant is also parent to several hybrids (''see table''). Of these, the most common is ''V.'' × ''semialbum'' Chaub. (× ''V. nigrum''). All occur in Eurasia, and three, ''V.'' × ''kerneri'' Fritsch, ''V.'' × ''pterocaulon'' Franch. and ''V.'' × ''thapsi'' L. ([[synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''V.'' × ''spurium'' W.D.J.Koch), have also been reported in North America.{{cite web |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=VERBA |title=''Verbascum'' L. |work=PLANTS Profile |publisher=USDA Natural resources Conservation Service |access-date=7 March 2007 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101119114746/http://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=VERBA |archive-date=19 November 2010 }} === Common names === ''V. thapsus'' is known by a variety of names. European reference books call it "great mullein".{{cite web |title=Great Mullein ''Verbascum thapsus'' Linnaeus |url=http://www.jncc.gov.uk/default.aspx?page=3316&SpeciesID=26550&type=species |work=Wildlife Statistics |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-date=28 September 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928003515/http://www.jncc.gov.uk/default.aspx?page=3316&SpeciesID=26550&type=species |url-status=dead }}[[#Watts|Watts (2000)]], pp. 633–634. In North America, "common mullein" is used{{cite book |last=Niering |first=William A. |title=The Audubon Society field guide to North American wildflowers, eastern region |location=New York |publisher=Knopf |year=1979 |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=798 }}{{cite encyclopedia |title=The Mulleins (Verbascum) |page=389 |encyclopedia=Wild Flowers of the United States |volume=1. The Northeastern States (Part 2) |year=1966 |editor=Harold William Rickett |location=New York |publisher=McGraw-Hill |lccn=66017920 }} while western United States residents sometimes refer to mullein as "cowboy toilet paper".{{cite web |title=Beyond the River |url=http://www.tpwmagazine.com/archive/2006/jan/ed_6/ |work=Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine |publisher=Dale Weisman |access-date=26 June 2010 |archive-date=30 November 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101130173145/http://tpwmagazine.com/archive/2006/jan/ed_6/ |url-status=live }}{{cite web |title=BIO 406D-Native Plants |url=http://www.sbs.utexas.edu/bio406d/packets/Fall%2005/F05-FT1-StEd.pdf |work=An Introduction to the Flora of Central Texas |publisher=Michael Gruenstaeudl |access-date=26 June 2010 |archive-date=14 May 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110514140541/http://www.sbs.utexas.edu/bio406d/packets/Fall%2005/F05-FT1-StEd.pdf |url-status=live }} In the 19th century, it had well over 40 different common names in English alone. Some of the more whimsical ones included "hig candlewick", "Indian rag weed", "bullicks lungwort", "Adams-rod", "hare's-beard", and "ice-leaf".{{Cite encyclopedia |last=Britton |first=Nathaniel A. |author2=Addison Brown |encyclopedia=An illustrated flora of the northern United States and Canada |volume=3. Gentianaceae to Compositae |year=1979 |publisher=Dover Publications |location=New York |page=175 |isbn=0-486-22644-1 |title=Illustrated Flora of the Northern United States and Canada }} Vernacular names include innumerable references to the plant's hairiness: “lamb’s ear”, "woolly mullein", "velvet mullein", or "blanket mullein",{{cite book |first1=Lois |last1=Brako |first2=Amy Y. |last2=Rossman |first3=David F. |last3=Farr |title=Scientific and common names of 7,000 vascular plants in the United States |year=1995 |location=St. Paul, Minnesota |publisher=APS Press |isbn=0-89054-171-X |page=189 }} "beggar's blanket", "Moses' blanket", "poor man's blanket", "Our Lady's blanket", or "old man's blanket",[[#Watts|Watts (2000)]], pp. 108, 369. and "feltwort", and so on ("flannel" is another common generic name). "Mullein" itself derives from the French word for "soft".{{cite web |url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/mullein |title=mullein (n.) |website=Etymonline }} Some names refer to the plant's size and shape: "shepherd's club(s)" or "staff", "[[Aaron's rod]]"{{Cite book |last1=Coutts |first1=J |title=The Complete Book of Gardening |last2=Osborn |first2=A |last3=Edwards |first3=A |publisher=Ward, Lock & Co., Limited |year=1954 |editor-last=Preston |editor-first=G.H. |location=Great Britain |pages=255 }} (a name it shares with a number of other plants with tall, yellow inflorescences), and a plethora of other "X's staff" and "X's rod".[[#Watts|Watts (2000)]], pp. 774–775, 819–820. p. 866: "A tall plant like Mullein attracts 'staff' and 'rod' names." The name "velvet dock" or "mullein dock" is also recorded, where "dock" is a British name applied to any broad-leaved plant.[[#Watts|Watts (2000)]], pp. 302, 634. Alongside Aaron's rod, ''Verbascum thapsus'' is sometimes referred to as Aaron's beard, a name it shares with several other plants.{{Cite encyclopedia |year=1961 |title=Aaron's Beard |encyclopedia=[[Everyman's Encyclopaedia]] |publisher=The Reprint Society London |editor-last=Bozman |editor-first=Ernest Franklin |editor-link=Ernest Franklin Bozman |volume=1 |pages=4 }} == Distribution and habitat == ''V. thapsus'' has a wide native range including Europe, northern Africa, and Asia, from the [[Azores]] and [[Canary Islands]] east to western China, north to the [[British Isles]], [[Scandinavia]], and [[Siberia]], [[Kashmir]]{{Cite journal |last=Ganie |first=Aijaz Hassan |date=8 December 2018 |title=Verbascum songaricum (Scrophulariaceae): An addition to the flora of India |url=http://rheedea.in/storages/submission/file/1073714543.pdf |journal=Rheedea |volume=28(2) |issue=111–113 |pages=3 }} and south to the [[Himalayas]].[http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Verbascum&SPECIES_XREF=thapsus Flora Europaea: ''Verbascum thapsus''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930221358/http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Verbascum&SPECIES_XREF=thapsus |date=30 September 2007 }}, retrieved on 6 November 2009.{{GRIN | access-date = 6 November 2009 }} In northern Europe, it grows from sea level up to 1,850 m altitude, while in China it grows at 1,400–3,200 m altitude. It has been introduced throughout the temperate world, and is [[naturalisation (biology)|established]] as a [[weed]] in Australia, New Zealand, tropical Asia, [[La Réunion]], North America, [[Hawaii]], Chile, [[Hispaniola]], and Argentina.{{cite web |title=Ficha de la Especie ''Verbascum thapsus'' |url=http://www.uns.edu.ar/inbiar/ver_especie.asp?especie_id=333 |work=Base de Datos sobre Invasiones Biológicas en Argentina |publisher=Universidad Nacional del Sur |access-date=6 November 2009 |language=es |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090715220411/http://www.uns.edu.ar/inbiar/ver_especie.asp?especie_id=333 |archive-date=15 July 2009 }}{{cite web |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' |url=http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=695 |date=8 July 2005 |work=Global Invasive Species Database |publisher=IUCN Invasive Species Specialist Group |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-date=15 July 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090715092435/http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=695 |url-status=dead }}{{cite web |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' |url=http://www.hear.org/Pier/species/verbascum_thapsus.htm |publisher=Hawaiian Ecosystems at Risk project |work=Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk |date=19 February 2007 |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-date=16 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091216122628/http://www.hear.org/Pier/species/verbascum_thapsus.htm |url-status=live }} It has also been reported in Japan.{{cite web |title=List of alien species recognized to be established in Japan or found in the Japanese wild (as of October 27, 2004) |url=http://www.env.go.jp/en/nature/as/041110.pdf |access-date=6 November 2009 |work=Japan Ministry of Environment |archive-date=26 March 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090326062622/http://www.env.go.jp/en/nature/as/041110.pdf |url-status=live }} In the United States, it was imported very early in the 18th{{refn|The 1630 number in Mitch may be a typo: the beginning of the 18th century is cited in other sources.|group=note}} century and cultivated for its medicinal and [[piscicide]] properties. By 1818, it had begun spreading so much that [[Amos Eaton]] thought it was a native plant.{{refn|Eaton went so far as to write: "When botanists are so infatuated with wild speculation, as to tell us the mullein was introduced, they give our youngest pupils occasion to sneer at their teachers."{{Cite book |last=Pennel |first=Francis Whittier |title=The Scrophulariaceae of eastern temperate North America |year=1935 |publisher=George W. Carpenter Fund |location=Philadelphia |pages=173–174 |oclc=852625 }}|group=note}}{{cite web |last=Mitch |first=Larry W. |title=Common Mullein—the Roadside Torch Parade |url=http://wssa.net/Weeds/ID/WorldOfWeeds/mullein.html |work=Intriguing World of Weeds |publisher=[[Weed Science Society of America]] |access-date=6 November 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090702071108/http://wssa.net/Weeds/ID/WorldOfWeeds/mullein.html |archive-date=2 July 2009 }} In 1839, it was already reported in [[Michigan]] and in 1876, in [[California]].{{cite web |first=Tom |last=Remaley |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' |url=http://www.nps.gov/plants/alien/fact/veth1.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19990428225117/http://www.nps.gov/plants/alien/fact/veth1.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=28 April 1999 |year=1998 |publisher=Plant Conservation Alliance's Alien Plant Working Group |access-date=6 November 2009 }} It is now found commonly in all the states.{{cite web |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=VETH |work=PLANTS Database |publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]] [[Natural Resources Conservation Service]] |access-date=6 November 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101016082110/http://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=VETH |archive-date=16 October 2010 }} In Canada, it is most common in the [[The Maritimes|Maritime Provinces]] and southern [[Quebec]], [[Ontario]], and [[British Columbia]], with scattered populations in between.{{cite web |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' |url=http://www.natureserve.org/explorer/servlet/NatureServe?searchName=verbascum+thapsus |work=NatureServe Explorer |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-date=11 May 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080511230943/http://www.natureserve.org/explorer/servlet/NatureServe?searchName=verbascum+thapsus |url-status=dead}}[], retrieved 29 December 2006. Great mullein most frequently grows as a colonist of bare and disturbed soil, usually on sandy or chalky ones. It grows best in dry, sandy, or gravelly soils, although it can grow in a variety of habitats, including banksides, meadows, roadsides, forest clearings, and pastures. This ability to grow in a wide range of habitats has been linked to strong [[Phenotype#Phenotypic variation|phenotype variation]] rather than [[adaptation]] capacities.{{cite journal |last=Parker |first=Ingrid M. |author2=Joseph Rodriguez |author3=Michael E. Loik |title=An Evolutionary Approach to Understanding the Biology of Invasions: Local Adaptation and General-Purpose Genotypes in the Weed ''Verbascum thapsus'' |journal=Conservation Biology |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=59–72 |date=February 2003 |doi=10.1046/j.1523-1739.2003.02019.x |bibcode=2003ConBi..17...59P |s2cid=18289261 }} == Ecology == [[Image:Starr 040723-0074 Verbascum thapsus.jpg|thumb|left|upright|alt=A Mullein plant growing in aa dry, mountainous area.|''V. thapsus'' grows best with little competition.]] Great mullein is a biennial and generally requires [[vernalization|winter dormancy]] before it can flower. This dormancy is linked to [[starch]] degradation activated by low temperatures in the root, and [[gibberellin]] application bypasses this requirement. Seeds germinate almost solely in bare soil, at temperatures between 10 and 40 °C. While they can germinate in total darkness if proper conditions are present (tests give a 35% germination rate under ideal conditions), in the wild, they in practice only do so when exposed to light, or very close to the soil surface, which explains the plant's habitat preferences. While it can also grow in areas where some vegetation already exists, growth of the rosettes on bare soil is four to seven times more rapid. Seeds germinate in spring and summer. Those that germinate in autumn produce plants that overwinter if they are large enough, while rosettes less than {{convert|15|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} across die in winter. After flowering, the entire plant usually dies at the end of its second year, but some individuals, especially in the northern parts of the range, require a longer growth period and flower in their third year. Under better growing conditions, some individuals flower in the first year.{{cite journal |last=Reinartz |first=James A. |title=Life History Variation of Common Mullein (''Verbascum Thapsus''): I. Latitudinal Differences in Population Dynamics and Timing of Reproduction |journal=The Journal of Ecology |volume=72 |issue=3 |date=November 1984 |pages=897–912 |issn=0022-0477 |doi=10.2307/2259539 |jstor=2259539 |bibcode=1984JEcol..72..897R }} Triennial individuals have been found to produce fewer seeds than biennial and annual ones. While year of flowering and size are linked to the environment, most other characteristics appear to be genetic.{{cite journal |last=Reinartz |first=James A. |title=Life History Variation of Common Mullein (''Verbascum Thapsus''): III. Differences Among Sequential Cohorts |journal=The Journal of Ecology |volume=72 |issue=3 |date=November 1984 |pages=927–936 |doi=10.2307/2259541 |jstor=2259541 |bibcode=1984JEcol..72..927R }} A given flower is open only for a single day, opening before dawn and closing in the afternoon. Flowers are [[reproduction#Autogamy|self-fecundating]] and [[Dichogamy|protogynous]] (with female parts maturing first), and will self-pollinate if they have not been [[pollination|pollinated]] by insects during the day. While many insects visit the flowers, only some bees actually accomplish pollination. The flowering period of ''V. thapsus'' lasts from June to August in most of its range, extending to September or October in warmer climates. Visitors include [[Halictidae|halictid]] bees and [[hoverfly|hoverflies]].{{cite web |last=Hilty |first=John |title=Great Mullein |url=http://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/weeds/plants/great_mullein.htm |work=Weedy Wildflowers of Illinois |publisher=Illinois Wildflowers |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-date=26 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090626052153/http://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/weeds/plants/great_mullein.htm |url-status=live }} The hair on lower stamens may serve to provide footholds for visitors. [[Image:Verbascum thapsus fruit kz.jpg|thumb|alt=A close-up of the green capsules of V. thapsus, surrounded by the sepals|The fruit of great mullein contains large numbers of minute seeds.]] The seeds maintain their germinative powers for decades, up to 100 years, according to some studies.{{Cite journal |last=Kivilaan |first=A. |author2=Robert S. Bandurski |title=The One Hundred-Year Period for Dr. Beal's Seed Viability Experiment |journal=American Journal of Botany |volume=69 |issue=9 |date=October 1981 |pages=1290–1292 |issn=0002-9122 |doi=10.2307/2443054 |jstor=2443054 }} Because of this, and because the plant is an extremely prolific seed bearer (each plant produces hundreds of capsules, each containing up to 700 seeds, with a total up to 180,000 or 240,000 seeds), it remains in the [[soil seed bank]] for extended periods of time, and can sprout from apparently bare ground, or shortly after [[forest fire]]s long after previous plants have died. Its population pattern typically consists of an ephemeral adult population followed by a long period of dormancy as seeds. Great mullein rarely establishes on new grounds without human intervention because its seeds do not disperse very far. [[biological dispersal|Seed dispersion]] requires the stem to be moved by wind or animal movement; 75% of the seeds fall within 1 m of the parent plant, and 93% fall within 5 m. [[Megachilidae|Megachilid]] bees of the genus ''[[Anthidium]]'' use the hair (amongst that of various woolly plants) in making their [[nest]]s.{{cite book |first=Paul |last=Westrich |year=1996 |chapter=Habitat requirements of central European bees and the problems of partial habitats |chapter-url=http://www.paul-westrich.de/downloads/westrich_40.pdf |editor=Matheson |display-editors=etal |title=The Conservation of Bees |series=Linnean Society Symposium Series, '''18''' |pages=1–16 |location=London |publisher=Academic Press |archive-date=19 July 2011 |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719071957/http://www.paul-westrich.de/downloads/westrich_40.pdf |url-status=live }} The seeds are generally too small for birds to feed on, although the [[American goldfinch]] has been reported to consume them.{{cite journal |last=Coutlee |first=Ellen L. |title=Maintenance Behavior of the American Goldfinch |url=http://sora.unm.edu/sites/default/files/journals/wilson/v075n04/p0342-p0357.pdf |journal=Wilson Bulletin |volume=75 |issue=4 |date=December 1963 |pages=342–357 |issn=0043-5643 |archive-date=11 September 2014 |access-date=4 April 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140911114417/http://sora.unm.edu/sites/default/files/journals/wilson/v075n04/p0342-p0357.pdf |url-status=live }} Other bird species have been reported to consume the leaves ([[Hawaiian goose]])Banko, Paul C., Black, Jeffrey M. and Banko, Winston E. (1999). [https://bna.birds.cornell.edu/bna/species/434/articles/introduction Hawaiian Goose (''Branta sandvicensis'')] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160805030419/http://bna.birds.cornell.edu/bna/species/434/articles/introduction |date=5 August 2016 }}, The Birds of North America Online (A. Poole, Ed.). Ithaca: Cornell Lab of Ornithology. or flowers ([[palila]]),Banko, Paul C. ''et al.'' (2002). [https://bna.birds.cornell.edu/bna/species/679/articles/introduction Palila (''Loxioides bailleui'')] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160805001757/http://bna.birds.cornell.edu/bna/species/679/articles/introduction |date=5 August 2016 }}, The Birds of North America Online (A. Poole, Ed.). Ithaca: Cornell Lab of Ornitholog. or to use the plant as a source when [[foraging]] for insects ([[white-headed woodpecker]]).Garrett, Kimball L., Raphael, Martin G. and Dixon, Rita D. (1996). [https://bna.birds.cornell.edu/bna/species/252/articles/introduction White-headed Woodpecker (''Picoides albolarvatus'')] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160805002259/http://bna.birds.cornell.edu/bna/species/252/articles/introduction |date=5 August 2016 }}, The Birds of North America Online (A. Poole, Ed.). Ithaca: Cornell Lab of Ornithology. Additionally, deer and elk eat the leaves.{{Cite book |last=Reiner |first=Ralph E. |title=Introducing the Flowering Beauty of Glacier National Park and the Majestic High Rockies |publisher=Glacier Park, Inc. |year=1969 |pages=42 }} ==Fossil record== Seeds of ''V. thapsus'' have been recorded from part of the [[Cromer Forest Bed]] series and at [[West Wittering]] in [[Sussex]] from some parts of the [[Ipswichian interglacial]] layers.The History of the British Flora, A Factual Basis for Phytogeography by [[Sir Harry Godwin]], Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, {{ISBN|0 521 20254 X}}, 1975 edition page 318 == Agricultural impacts and control == Because it cannot compete with established plants, great mullein is no longer considered a serious agricultural weed and is easily crowded out in cultivation,{{Cite journal |last=Gross |first=Katherine L. |author2=Patricia A. Werner |title=The Biology of Canadian Weeds. 28. ''Verbascum thapsus'' L. and ''V. blattaria'' L |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |volume=58 |pages=401–413 |date=April 1978 |doi=10.4141/cjps78-062 |issue=2 |doi-access=free}} Reprinted in Mulligan, G.A. (1979), ''The Biology of Canadian Weeds'' I, {{ISBN|0-662-10668-7}}, pp. 320–331. except in areas where vegetation is sparse to begin with, such as [[California]]n semidesertic areas of the eastern [[Sierra Nevada (U.S.)|Sierra Nevada]] in the USA. In such ecological contexts, it crowds out native herbs and grasses; its tendency to appear after forest fires also disturbs the normal [[ecological succession]]. Although not an agricultural threat, its presence can be very difficult to eradicate and is especially problematic in [[overgrazing|overgrazed]] pastures.{{Cite web |last=Pitcairn |first=Michael |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' |url=http://www.cal-ipc.org/ip/management/ipcw/pages/detailreport.cfm@usernumber=87&surveynumber=182.php |work=Invasive Plants of California's Wildland |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110312005513/http://www.cal-ipc.org/ip/management/ipcw/pages/detailreport.cfm%40usernumber%3D87%26surveynumber%3D182.php |archive-date=12 March 2011 }} The species is legally listed as a [[noxious weed]] in the US state of [[Colorado]] (class C){{cite web |title=Colorado State-listed Noxious Weeds |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/noxious?rptType=State&statefips=08 |work=PLANTS Database |publisher=USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service |access-date=6 November 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090702071108/http://plants.usda.gov/java/noxious?rptType=State&statefips=08 |archive-date=2 July 2009 }} and Hawaii,{{cite web |title=Hawaii State-listed Noxious Weeds |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/noxious?rptType=State&statefips=15 |work=PLANTS Database |publisher=USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service |access-date=6 November 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101008175302/http://plants.usda.gov/java/noxious?rptType=State&statefips=15 |archive-date=8 October 2010 }} and the Australian state of [[Victoria, Australia|Victoria]] (regionally prohibited in the [[West Gippsland]] region, and regionally controlled in several others).{{cite web |last=Faithful |first=Ian |title=Great Mullein |url=http://www.dpi.vic.gov.au/dpi/nreninf.nsf/LinkView/D2FE171D9ECA1CC9CA256BCF000AD563ECC844336D72F0634A256DEA00293F8A |publisher=Victoria Department of Primary Industries |access-date=6 November 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110315090054/http://www.dpi.vic.gov.au/dpi/nreninf.nsf/LinkView/D2FE171D9ECA1CC9CA256BCF000AD563ECC844336D72F0634A256DEA00293F8A |archive-date=15 March 2011 }} Despite not being an agricultural weed in itself, it [[Host (biology)|hosts]] a number of insects and [[disease]]s, including both [[pest (organism)|pests]] and [[beneficial insects]].{{cite journal |last=Horton |first=David R. |author2=Tamera M. Lewis |date=December 2003 |title=Numbers and types of arthropods overwintering on common mullein, ''Verbascum thapsus'' L. (Scrophulariaceae), in a central Washington fruit-growing region |journal=Journal of the Entomological Society of British Columbia |volume=100 |pages=79–86 |issn=0071-0733 |url=https://www.sfu.ca/biology/esbc/Journal/journal2003/2003_Horton.pdf |access-date=6 November 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101016082110/http://www.sfu.ca/biology/esbc/Journal/journal2003/2003_Horton.pdf |archive-date=16 October 2010 }} It is also a potential reservoir of the [[cucumber mosaic virus]], ''[[Erysiphum cichoraceum]]'' (the cucurbit [[powdery mildew]]) and [[Texas root rot]].{{cite journal |last=Price |first=W. C. |title=Comparative Host Ranges of Six Plant Viruses |journal=American Journal of Botany |date=July 1940 |volume=57 |issue=7 |pages=530–541 |issn=0002-9122 |doi=10.2307/2437088 |jstor=2437088 }} A study found ''V. thapsus'' hosts insects from 29 different [[Family (taxonomy)|families]]. Most of the pests found were [[western flower thrips]] (''Frankliniella occidentalis''), ''[[Lygus]]'' species such as the [[tarnished plant bug]] (''L. lineolaris''), and various spider mites from the family [[Tetranychidae]]. These make the plant a potential reservoir for [[overwintering]] pests. Other insects commonly found on great mullein feed exclusively on ''Verbascum'' species in general or ''V. thapsus'' in particular. They include mullein thrips (''[[Haplothrips]] verbasci''), ''[[Gymnaetron tetrum]]'' (whose larva consume the seeds), and the [[mullein moth]] (''Cucullia verbasci''). Useful insects are also hosted by great mullein, including predatory mites of the genera ''[[Galendromus]]'', ''[[Typhlodromus]]'', and ''[[Amblyseius]]'', the [[minute pirate bug]] ''Orius tristicolor'', and the mullein bug (''[[Campylomma verbasci]]'').{{cite web |last=Higbee |first=Bradley S. |title=Campylomma verbasci (Meyer) |url=https://www.biocontrol.entomology.cornell.edu/predators/Campylomma.html |work=Biological Control: A Guide to Natural Enemies in North America |publisher=[[Cornell University]] |access-date=21 December 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120425175203/http://www.biocontrol.entomology.cornell.edu/predators/Campylomma.html |archive-date=25 April 2012 }} The plant's ability to host both pests and beneficials makes it potentially useful to maintain stable populations of insects used for biological control in other cultures, like ''Campylomma verbasci'' and ''[[Dicyphus hesperus]]'' ([[Miridae]]), a predator of [[whitefly|whiteflies]].{{cite web |last=Ferguson |first=Gillian |date=26 September 2005 |title=Can ''Dicyphus hesperus'' control whiteflies in greenhouse tomatoes? |url=http://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/crops/facts/dicyphus.htm |publisher=Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs |access-date=6 November 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060127011547/http://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/crops/facts/dicyphus.htm |archive-date=27 January 2006 }}{{cite journal |last=Sanchez |first=Juan Antonio |author2=David R. Gillespie |author3=Robert R. McGregor |title=The effects of mullein plants (''Verbascum thapsus'') on the population dynamics of ''Dicyphus hesperus'' (Heteroptera: Miridae) in tomato greenhouses |journal=Biological Control |volume=28 |issue=3 |date=November 2003 |pages=313–319 |doi=10.1016/S1049-9644(03)00116-6 |bibcode=2003BiolC..28..313S }} A number of pest [[Lepidoptera]] species, including the [[stalk borer]] (''Papaipema nebris'') and [[gray hairstreak]] (''Strymon melinus''), also use ''V. thapsus'' as a host plant.{{cite web |title=HOSTS – a Database of the World's Lepidopteran Hostplants |url=http://avalanche.nhm.ac.uk/jdsml/research-curation/projects/hostplants//list.dsml?searchPageURL=index.dsml&Familyqtype=starts+with&Family=&PFamilyqtype=starts+with&PFamily=&Genusqtype=starts+with&Genus=&PGenusqtype=starts+with&PGenus=verbascum&Speciesqtype=starts+with&PSpeciesqtype=starts+with&PSpecies=thapsus&sort=Family |publisher=The [[Natural History Museum, London|Natural History Museum]] |access-date=6 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080627170707/http://avalanche.nhm.ac.uk/jdsml/research-curation/projects/hostplants//list.dsml?searchPageURL=index.dsml&Familyqtype=starts%2Bwith&Family=&PFamilyqtype=starts%2Bwith&PFamily=&Genusqtype=starts%2Bwith&Genus=&PGenusqtype=starts%2Bwith&PGenus=verbascum&Speciesqtype=starts%2Bwith&PSpeciesqtype=starts%2Bwith&PSpecies=thapsus&sort=Family |archive-date=27 June 2008 |url-status=dead }} [[Image:Starr 040723-0032 Verbascum thapsus.jpg|thumb|upright|alt=A series of leaves is seen wrapping down the length of a stem. The leaves have thick veining and both they and the stem have a woolly appearance from the hair covering them.|Because of ample irritating hair, ''V. thapsus'' is resistant to grazing and contact herbicides.]] Control of the plant, when desired, is best managed via mechanical means, such as hand pulling and hoeing, preferably followed by sowing of native plants. Animals rarely [[grazing|graze]] it because of its irritating hairs, and liquid [[herbicide]]s require [[surfactant]]s to be effective, as the hair causes water to roll off the plant, much like the [[lotus effect]]. Burning is ultimately ineffective, as it only creates new bare areas for [[seedling]]s to occupy. ''G. tetrum'' and ''Cucullia verbasci'' usually have little effect on ''V. thapsus'' populations as a whole. Goats and chickens have also been proposed to control mullein. Effective (when used with a surfactant) contact herbicides include [[glyphosate]], [[triclopyr]] and [[sulfurometuron-methyl]]. Ground herbicides, like [[tebuthiuron]], are also effective, but they result in bare ground – ideal conditions for growing more mullein – and therefore require repeated application to prevent regrowth. == Uses == ===Phytochemicals=== [[Phytochemical]]s in ''V. thapsus'' flowers and leaves include [[saponin]]s, [[polysaccharide]]s, [[mucilage]], [[flavonoid]]s, [[tannin]]s, [[iridoid]] and [[lignin]] [[glycoside]]s, and [[essential oil]]s. The plant's leaves, in addition to the seeds, have been reported to contain [[rotenone]], although quantities are unknown.{{cite web |title=''Verbascum thapsus'' |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Verbascum_thapsus |publisher=Plants For A Future |access-date=16 March 2011 |archive-date=13 May 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110513204152/http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Verbascum_thapsus |url-status=live }} === Traditional medicine === [[File:Verbasci flos dried.jpg|thumb|"Verbasci flos": dried flowers of ''V. thapsus'' as used in herbal tea]] Although long used in [[herbal medicine]], no [[prescription drug|drugs]] are manufactured from its components. [[Pedanius Dioscorides|Dioscorides]] first recommended the plant 2000 years ago, considering it useful as a [[traditional medicine|folk medicine]] for pulmonary diseases.{{cite book |last=Silverman |first=Maida |year=1977 |title=A City Herbal: Lore, Legend, & Uses of Common Weeds |chapter=Mullein |chapter-url=http://www.ashtreepublishing.com/Book_City_Herbal_Mullen.htm |pages=[https://archive.org/details/cityherballorele00silv/page/99 99–104] |isbn=1-888123-00-1 |publisher=Ash Tree Publishing |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/cityherballorele00silv/page/99 }} Leaves were smoked to attempt to treat lung ailments, a tradition that in America was rapidly transmitted to [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]] peoples.{{cite encyclopedia |last=Grieve |first=Margaret |encyclopedia=A Modern Herbal |title=Mullein, Great |orig-year=1931 |year=1982 |url=http://botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/m/mulgre63.html |access-date=6 November 2009 |location=New York |publisher=Dover Publication |volume=2: I-Z |isbn=0-486-22799-5 |archive-date=3 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091103021512/http://www.botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/m/mulgre63.html |url-status=live }}{{cite encyclopedia |last=Hanrahan |first=Claire |author2=Rebecca J. Frey |editor=Jacqueline L. Longe |encyclopedia=The Gale encyclopedia of alternative medicine |title=Mullein |url=http://enotes.com/alternative-medicine-encyclopedia/mullein |access-date=30 November 2006 |edition=2nd |year=2005 |publisher=Thomson Gale |volume=3: L-R |location=Detroit |isbn=0-7876-7427-3 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090715111125/http://enotes.com/alternative-medicine-encyclopedia/mullein |archive-date=15 July 2009 }} The [[Zuni people]], however, use the plant in [[poultice]]s of powdered root applied to [[Ulcer (dermatology)|sore]]s, [[rash]]es, and skin infections. An infusion of the root is also used to treat [[athlete's foot]].{{cite journal |last1=Camzine |first1=Scott |first2=Robert A. |last2=Bye |year=1980 |title=A Study Of The Medical Ethnobotany Of The Zuni Indians of New Mexico |journal=[[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]] |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=365–388;378 |doi=10.1016/S0378-8741(80)81017-8 |pmid=6893476 }} All preparations meant to be drunk have to be finely filtered to eliminate the irritating hairs.{{Cite journal |last=Turker |first=Arzu Ucar |author2=Ekrem Gurel |title=Common Mullein (''Verbascum thapsus'' L.): Recent Advances in Research |journal=Phytotherapy Research |volume=19 |issue=9 |date=September 2005 |pages=733–739 |doi=10.1002/ptr.1653 |pmid=16222647 |s2cid=11961736 |url=http://www.drlowdog.com/Assets/pdf_files/FIHM_online_docs/fihm_part_3/fihm_11_respiratory_system/Handouts/mullein_Review.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150213075134/http://www.drlowdog.com/Assets/pdf_files/FIHM_online_docs/fihm_part_3/fihm_11_respiratory_system/Handouts/mullein_Review.pdf |archive-date=13 February 2015 }} Oil from the flowers was used against [[catarrh]]s, [[colic]]s, [[earache]]s, [[frostbite]], [[eczema]], and other external conditions. Topical application of various ''V. thapsus''-based preparations was recommended for the treatment of [[wart]]s,{{cite journal |last=Drury |first=Susan |title=Plants and Wart Cures in England from the Seventeenth to the Nineteenth Century: Some Examples |journal=Folklore |volume=102 |issue=1 |year=1991 |pages=97–100 |jstor=1260360 |doi=10.1080/0015587X.1991.9715809 }} [[Boil (infection)|boil]]s, [[carbuncle (pathology)|carbuncle]]s, hemorrhoids, and [[chilblain]]s, amongst others. [[Glycyrrhizin]] compounds with [[bactericide]] effects in vitro were isolated from flowers.{{cite journal |last=Turker |first=Arzu Ucar |author2=N. D. Camper |title=Biological activity of common mullein, a medicinal plant |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |date=October 2002 |volume=82 |issue=2–3 |pages=117–125 |doi=10.1016/S0378-8741(02)00186-1 |pmid=12241986 }} The German [[Commission E]] describes uses of the plant for respiratory infections.{{cite web |title=Mullein flower |url=http://www.herbalgram.org/iherb/commissione/Monographs/Monograph_0262.html |work=The Commission E Monographs |date=1 February 1990 |publisher=American Botanical Council |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060511234235/http://www.herbalgram.org/iherb/commissione/Monographs/Monograph_0262.html |archive-date=11 May 2006 |access-date=6 November 2009 }} It was also part of the [[National Formulary]] in the United States and United Kingdom. The plant has been used in an attempt to treat colds, [[croup]], sunburn, and other skin irritations. === Other uses === Roman soldiers are said to have dipped the plant stalks in grease for use as torches. Other cultures use the leaves as wicks.{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering |last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-year=1979 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=653 }} Native Americans and American colonists lined their shoes with leaves from the plant to keep out the cold. Mullein may be cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]]. As with many plants, ([[Pliny the Elder]] described it in his ''[[Natural History (Pliny)|Naturalis Historia]]''),{{refn|In book 25, Pliny describes "two principal kinds [of verbascum]" thought to be ''V. thapsus'' and ''V. sinuatum''. The precise attribution of a third kind is unclear.[https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/cgi-bin/ptext?doc=Perseus:text:1999.02.0138&query=chapter%3D%232114 Latin] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080511152842/http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/cgi-bin/ptext?doc=Perseus:text:1999.02.0138&query=chapter%3D%232114 |date=11 May 2008 }}, [https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/cgi-bin/ptext?doc=Perseus:text:1999.02.0137%3Ahead%3D%231784 English] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080511152839/http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/cgi-bin/ptext?doc=Perseus:text:1999.02.0137:head= |date=11 May 2008 }}|group=note}} great mullein was linked to [[witch]]es, although the relationship remained generally ambiguous, and the plant was also widely held to ward off [[curse]]s and [[evil spirit]]s. The seeds contain several compounds ([[saponin]]s, [[glycoside]]s, [[coumarin]], [[rotenone]]) that are toxic to fish, and have been widely used as [[piscicide]] for [[fishing]].{{Cite journal |last=Wilhelm |first=Gene |title=The mullein: Plant piscicide of the mountain folk culture |journal=[[Geographical Review]] |volume=64 |issue=2 |pages=235–252 |date=April 1974 |doi=10.2307/213812 |jstor=213812 |bibcode=1974GeoRv..64..235W }} Due to its weedy capacities, the plant, unlike other species of the genus (such as ''[[Verbascum phoeniceum|V. phoeniceum]]''), is not often cultivated. == Gallery == File:00 2262 Kleinblütige Königskerze (Verbascum thapsus).gif File:Great Mullein (Verbascum thapsus) -
